source.title: On some open problems of number theory

accepted.question_text: A positive integer is perfect when it is equal to the sum of all of its proper divisors. Is the set of even perfect numbers infinite?
A positive integer is perfect when it is equal to the sum of all of its proper divisors. Is there any odd perfect number?
For a positive integer n, let s(n) be the sum of all proper divisors of n. Two positive integers m < n are amicable if s(m) = n and s(n) = m. Are there infinitely many amicable pairs?
Is every even integer greater than 2 representable as the sum of two prime numbers?

Call a positive integer d a numerus idoneus, or convenient number, if every odd integer that is essentially uniquely representable in the form x^2 + d y^2 and whose unique representation satisfies gcd(x, d y) = 1 is prime. Is there any such d greater than 1848?
Are there infinitely many twin-prime pairs, meaning pairs of primes p and q with q - p = 2?
Are there infinitely many prime numbers of the form x^2 + 1, with x an integer?
Let pi(x) count the primes at most x, and let li(x) denote the logarithmic integral. Does there exist a constant A such that every positive x satisfies |pi(x) - li(x)| < A sqrt(x) log x?
accepted.context_brief: von Koch form of the Riemann hypothesis

accepted.question_text: For every positive integer n, is there a prime number strictly between the consecutive squares n^2 and (n + 1)^2?
For a positive integer n, let s(n) be the sum of all proper divisors of n, and set s(0) = 0. For every positive integer n, is the iterated sequence n, s(n), s(s(n)), and so on bounded?
Let phi(n) be Euler's totient function, the number of positive integers at most n that are coprime to n. Is there an integer m for which the equation phi(x) = m has exactly one integer solution x?
When positive perfect powers are arranged in increasing order, must the difference between consecutive terms tend to infinity?
For every integer n > 1, does the equation 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z have a solution in positive integers x, y, and z?

A finite system of congruences x congruent to a_i modulo m_i is covering if every integer x satisfies at least one congruence in the system. Does there exist a covering system whose moduli m_i are all distinct odd integers greater than 1?
